name: Critical Thinking Skills
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Thinking Before You Believe
lesson.summary: This section introduces critical thinking as a concrete set of cognitive habits ,  checking logic, weighing evidence, spotting bias, reasoning in probabilities, and revising beliefs ,  that you will use throughout the book to evaluate quantum computing claims.
lesson.body:
Before you can evaluate any claim about quantum computers ,  that one will "break all encryption," that another "proves consciousness is quantum," that a startup's chip is "1000 times faster than a supercomputer" ,  you need a working toolkit for deciding what to believe and how strongly to believe it. That toolkit is critical thinking, and it is not a personality trait or a vague attitude of doubt. It is a small set of skills you can practice: checking whether an argument's conclusion actually follows from its premises, judging how good the evidence behind a claim really is, noticing when your own preferences are distorting your judgment, thinking in probabilities rather than certainties, and being willing to change your mind when new information arrives.

Start with logic. An argument can be perfectly valid in structure while still being false, because validity only concerns whether the conclusion follows from the premises ,  it says nothing about whether the premises are true. "If a technology is new, it must be revolutionary; quantum computing is new; therefore quantum computing is revolutionary" is a valid argument shape, but the first premise is simply not true, so the conclusion doesn't follow in reality. Learning to isolate the premises of a claim, rather than reacting to its overall impression, is the first move of critical thinking.

Next comes evidence assessment: not all support for a claim carries equal weight. A single enthusiastic anecdote, a press release, and a peer-reviewed, replicated experiment are not interchangeable forms of evidence, even though they can all be cited as "proof." Ask where a number came from, whether anyone else has reproduced the result, and whether the source has something to gain from you believing it. A claim repeated by ten news outlets that all cite the same original press release is still just one piece of evidence, not ten.

Bias recognition is the skill of noticing when your own mind is doing the arguing for you. Confirmation bias makes you notice and remember information that supports what you already want to believe, while similar counter-evidence slides past unnoticed. In an area as hyped and jargon-heavy as quantum computing, this bias runs in both directions: people excited about the technology overweight favorable claims, and people who distrust it overweight dismissive ones. Recognizing bias doesn't mean having no opinions; it means holding them loosely enough to notice when you're defending them rather than examining them.

Probabilistic thinking means treating most real-world claims as more or less likely rather than simply true or false, and adjusting that likelihood as evidence accumulates. If a single small trial reports a striking result, the right response is not full belief or full rejection, but a moderate shift in confidence that gets revised further once larger or repeated trials come in. This is exactly the mental habit you'll need for quantum computing, where early results are often small-scale, hardware is noisy, and headlines routinely outrun what the underlying data can support.

Finally, all of this only matters if you're willing to update. Critical thinking isn't a one-time judgment you render and defend forever; it's an ongoing process of revising your confidence as better evidence arrives, which is different from either stubbornness or reflexive doubt. Keeping that willingness alive is what will let you follow the more technical material ahead without either swallowing the hype or dismissing it out of hand.
